title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
extended_summary:
This study asks whether a short AI literacy intervention can reduce high school students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors motivate the work by arguing that as large language models are introduced into education, students may accept AI outputs uncritically, which could undermine critical thinking and learning. The paper focuses on reliance behavior rather than literacy outcomes such as reading comprehension, and it does not report subgroup or accessibility analyses.

The intervention was a short educational text about ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations and risks, and how to use it wisely. A control group read a shorter introductory text about ChatGPT without the literacy-focused content. Participants were 12th-grade students in Estonia, randomly assigned to intervention or control conditions in an online survey experiment. After reading, they completed self-reported AI literacy items and then solved eight math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect.

The main findings were that students showed substantial over-reliance overall, adopting incorrect recommendations about half the time. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance; instead, it increased under-reliance, meaning students were more likely to ignore correct recommendations after the literacy text. The intervention also increased students’ self-reported understanding of ChatGPT’s working mechanism and usage, but not limitations. The authors conclude that brief AI literacy texts may not be sufficient to reduce reliance on flawed LLM advice among secondary students.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model/chatbot used for text-based question answering, content generation, and recommendation of responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in a randomized experiment read a short AI literacy text about ChatGPT and then solved math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations; the study tested whether the intervention reduced adoption of incorrect ChatGPT recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison of an intervention text versus a control text (n=36), the mean over-reliance rate was lower in the intervention group (M=48.68, SD=24.26) than in the control group (M=55.88, SD=33.69), but the difference was not statistically significant, t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25. The authors report widespread over-reliance overall (52.1% of cases), but the intervention did not reduce over-reliance.
findings.measure: Over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations during math puzzle solving

findings.finding_summary: The intervention increased under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations: intervention group M=36.84 (SD=24.11) versus control group M=19.12 (SD=20.78), t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78. The paper interprets this as a moderate-to-large effect indicating greater tendency to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations after the literacy text.
findings.measure: Under-reliance on correct ChatGPT recommendations during math puzzle solving

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported AI literacy increased for 'Usage' and 'Working mechanism' after the intervention. Usage ratings were higher in the intervention group (M=3.42, SD=0.77) than control (M=2.77, SD=0.97), t(34)=2.26, p=.030, d=0.76; Working mechanism ratings were also higher in the intervention group (M=3.37, SD=0.76) than control (M=2.77, SD=0.90), t(34)=2.09, p=.044, d=0.70.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived knowledge of ChatGPT usage and working mechanism

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported knowledge about ChatGPT limitations did not differ significantly between groups: intervention M=2.95 (SD=0.91) versus control M=2.77 (SD=1.03), t(34)=0.56, p=.577, d=0.19. Thus, the intervention did not clearly improve participants' perceived understanding of limitations and risks.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived knowledge of ChatGPT limitations and risks

findings.finding_summary: Participants' confidence in their answers after using ChatGPT was slightly lower in the intervention group (M=3.58, SD=0.46) than in the control group (M=3.67, SD=0.76), but the difference was not statistically significant, U=188.50, p=.400, rrb=0.17.
findings.measure: Self-perceived confidence after relying on ChatGPT recommendations

findings.finding_summary: Initial decision time across puzzles did not differ significantly between groups. The intervention group had mean dttotal=1.56 minutes (SD=0.77) versus control mean dttotal=1.64 minutes (SD=1.12), U=179.5, p=.560. The authors use this to argue that the intervention did not measurably increase slow, analytical thinking.
findings.measure: Initial decision time across all puzzles

findings.finding_summary: Within-person correlations showed that longer initial decision times were associated with less over-reliance on incorrect recommendations (rs=-0.41, p=.013) and more under-reliance on correct recommendations (rs=0.35, p=.038). This suggests a tradeoff: slower deliberation reduced acceptance of wrong advice but also increased rejection of correct advice.
findings.measure: Correlation between decision time and reliance outcomes

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled experiment with a clear comparison group and pre-specified outcome measures, which supports relatively strong internal validity. However, the sample is very small and subgroup analyses were not reported, so confidence is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a large positive self-reported literacy effect for some measures (d=0.70-0.76) and a large negative effect on under-reliance (d=0.78), meeting the threshold for medium/large impact. The main target outcome, over-reliance, did not improve significantly.
